newsitem.title: USA: Dole sells economic plan in the South.
newsitem.headline: Dole sells economic plan in the South.

text.p: Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole charged on Monday that President Bill Clinton's policies were raising interest rates and pricing Americans out of the housing market.

During a "Listening to America" question-and-answer session at a home construction site in an Atlanta suburb, Dole said interest rates had risen 1.5 percent since Clinton vetoed a Republican balanced budget plan last year.

He said his ambitious proposal for a balanced federal budget and a 15 percent income tax cut would boost the economy and cut interest rates. "The government can help by lowering interest rates, lowering our federal spending, lowering the taxes and giving you an American opportunity, an opportunity to restore the American dream," he said.

Dole said economists have predicted interest rates would drop two percentage points if the federal budget were balanced, translating into tens of thousands of dollars in savings on a typical home mortgage.

He again vowed to balance the budget and cut taxes without cutting Medicare and other popular programmes. Democrats have charged that Dole's plan would dramatically increase the deficit, forcing deep cuts in Medeicare.
Dole ridiculed Clinton's plan for a package of targeted tax cuts, saying, "The trouble with his targeted tax cuts, they never hit anybody."
Dole also suggested he would unveil a new college student aid proposal, based on the GI Bill. Aides had no details.

Standing in shirtsleeves on a plywood platform in the sweltering heat, Dole was surrounded by bricks, roofing material and construction equipment and a sign reading "Tax Cuts Build Homes." He has tried to make the case the U.S. economy is soft, with stagnant wages, too many layoffs and slow overall growth.

U.S. housing starts were 1.455 million on an annual basis in July, however, up slightly from a year ago. A new report released on Monday also found businesss layoffs were at the lowest level in the past 16 months.

Some Federal Reserve policymakers are concerned the economy is growing too fast for its own good. There is speculation the central bank may raise rates to cool off the economy when it meets on Sept. 24.
Interest rates on 30-year government bonds have risen in recent months and are now over 7 percent. Those rates are benchmark for home mortgages.

From Georgia, Dole planned to travel to Tampa, Florida. Polls show Clinton, who spent two days campaigning in Florida last week, has a shot at winning the state in November, which would make him the first Democrat to do so in two decades.

Speaking to reporters on his plane, Dole said he was preparing for a series of debates with Clinton, tentatively scheduled to begin this month. He said representatives of his campaign would begin meeting with Clinton's camp on Thursday to work out details.

Dole said he had not started rehearsing for the debates. Asked how he felt about reports former Senate Democratic Leader George Mitchell would play Dole in Clinton practice sessions, he said, "Well, we're pretty good friends, maybe he'll help me out."

Recent public opinion polls have shown Clinton, who begins a three-day campaign swing of his own on Monday, holding a double-digit lead. They also show many Americans are sceptical that Dole's economic plan will work.
